title: From CTC to Take-Home: Checking a Salary Offer With Three Free Calculators
seoTitle: CTC to Take-Home Salary: A 2026 Calculator Guide
metaDescription: A ₹9,00,000 CTC is not ₹75,000 a month. Work the gap step by step with three free calculators, plus what the new labour codes change about your basic pay.
excerpt: A ₹9,00,000 offer is not ₹75,000 a month in hand, and the gap is entirely predictable once you know what sits in it. This tutorial works a real offer through three free calculators, then covers what the labour codes change about basic pay and PF.

faq.question: Why is my take-home so much lower than my CTC?
faq.answer: Because cost to company includes employer contributions and provisions that never reach your account, and your own deductions come out of what is left. In the worked example here a ₹9,00,000 package pays about ₹69,016 a month, and roughly ₹43,200 of the annual gap is provident fund that remains yours.

faq.question: Is employee provident fund calculated on basic salary or on a ceiling?
faq.answer: Many employers contribute twelve per cent of the statutory wage ceiling rather than of actual basic pay, which keeps the monthly figure fixed. Others contribute on full basic, which raises both sides. Ask which method your employer uses, because it changes your net pay noticeably.

faq.question: Do the new labour codes reduce take-home pay?
faq.answer: For anyone whose structure ran a low basic and a large allowance, usually yes, because a higher basic raises provident fund and gratuity contributions. Total cost to company need not change. The money moves from monthly pay into retirement savings rather than disappearing.

faq.question: Which tax regime should I use in the calculator?
faq.answer: Run both. The new regime has a higher standard deduction and a rebate that removes tax entirely at moderate incomes, while the old regime can still win where housing, insurance and interest deductions are large. Confirm the outcome with your CA before you elect one.

faq.question: Does professional tax apply everywhere in India?
faq.answer: No. It is a state levy, so the amount depends on where you are employed and several states do not charge it at all. Set it to your own state in the calculator rather than accepting a default.

bodyHtml:
An offer letter says ₹9,00,000. The candidate does the obvious sum, expects seventy-five thousand a month, and is disappointed in week five when the first payslip lands near sixty-nine. Nobody lied. The two numbers are measuring different things, and the gap between them is entirely predictable if you know what sits in it.

This is a walkthrough of that gap using three free calculators — the Take-Home Salary Calculator, the Income Tax Calculator and the Gratuity Calculator — run in that order. It is written for whoever is doing the arithmetic: a candidate checking an offer, or an owner building one and wanting to know what it really costs.

This is general information, not tax or legal advice. Slabs, thresholds and state rules change, and your own facts matter. Confirm anything here with your CA before you rely on it.

What cost to company actually contains

Cost to company is the employer's total annual cost of having you on the payroll. It is a budgeting figure, and it includes several things that are genuine costs to the business but never appear in anybody's bank account.

  • Gross salary — basic, house rent allowance, and whatever allowances the structure carries. This is the only part that is even potentially yours.
  • The employer's provident fund contribution — real money, paid into your retirement account rather than to you.
  • A gratuity provision — money set aside against a payment you receive only if you stay long enough to qualify.
  • Group insurance and benefits — premiums the business pays on your behalf.

Then, from the gross salary, come the deductions that reduce what reaches you: your own provident fund share, state-level professional tax where it applies, employee state insurance if your gross is below the notified wage limit, and income tax deducted at source.

Two arrows pointing in opposite directions, and the offer letter shows you only the top of the first one. That is why the calculators run in a specific order rather than all at once.

Step one: split the cost into employer costs and gross salary

Ask for the structure, not just the number. A reasonable employer will give you a component breakdown on request, and if nobody can produce one, that is information too.

Work from a ₹9,00,000 offer — ₹75,000 a month — with a fairly ordinary structure:

ComponentMonthlyAnnual
Basic₹35,000₹4,20,000
House rent allowance₹17,500₹2,10,000
Special allowance₹18,516₹2,22,192
Gross salary₹71,016₹8,52,192
Employer provident fund₹1,800₹21,600
Gratuity provision₹1,684₹20,208
Group insurance₹500₹6,000
Cost to company₹75,000₹9,00,000

The provident fund figure here is twelve per cent of the statutory wage ceiling of ₹15,000 rather than of the full basic, which is what many employers apply. Some contribute on actual basic instead, which raises both the employer cost and your deduction. There has been long-running pressure to raise that ceiling and it has not moved yet — check where it stands before you model a number that depends on it.

Before leaving this step, run the basic through the Gratuity Calculator. A ₹20,208 annual provision is not free money: it buys a payment that arrives only after you have completed the qualifying service. Seeing what it would actually pay out after five years tells you whether that line in the cost to company is worth anything to you.

Step two: subtract the statutory deductions

Feed the gross salary into the Take-Home Salary Calculator. Three deductions apply here, and only one of them is large.

Provident fund, employee share. Twelve per cent again, ₹1,800 a month on the ceiling basis. It leaves your pay but not your net worth — it is savings, not a cost, which is worth remembering before you resent it.

Professional tax. A state levy, and the amount depends entirely on where you work. A couple of hundred rupees a month is typical in the states that charge it; several states charge nothing. Take ₹200 for this example.

Employee state insurance. Applies only where gross pay is at or below the notified wage limit, which is well under the gross in this example, so it does not arise here. For lower-paid roles it does, and it is a meaningful deduction.

That gives ₹71,016 less ₹1,800 less ₹200, or ₹69,016 a month before income tax.

Step three: work out the tax

Now the Income Tax Calculator, on the annual gross of ₹8,52,192. Under the new regime as it has stood for the 2025-26 year: no tax up to ₹4,00,000, a salaried standard deduction of ₹75,000, and a rebate under section 87A that takes the liability to nil for total income up to ₹12,00,000.

Taxable income is ₹8,52,192 less ₹75,000, or ₹7,77,192. Tax at five per cent on the slice above ₹4,00,000 works out near ₹18,900 — and the rebate removes it. Nil.

So the honest answer for this offer is ₹69,016 a month in hand, against a headline of ₹75,000. A gap of ₹71,808 a year, of which ₹43,200 is provident fund that is still yours and ₹26,208 is provision and premium that is not.

Change the offer to something above the rebate threshold and the shape changes completely: tax becomes the largest single deduction and the gap between cost to company and take-home widens sharply. Run your own figure rather than scaling this one — the rebate makes the relationship anything but proportional. And check the slabs for the year you are actually in. They have moved at recent Budgets and will move again.

It is worth running the sum backwards too. If a candidate has told you the monthly figure they need, do not add a rough twenty per cent and call it a package. Start from the take-home they want, add back professional tax and the employee provident fund share to get the gross, then add the employer contribution, the gratuity provision and the insurance premium to get the cost to company. On this structure a ₹69,016 target lands at ₹9,00,000 — but the same target in a state with no professional tax, or under an employer who contributes on full basic, produces a different package entirely. The reverse calculation takes two minutes and stops the negotiation that otherwise happens twice.

What the labour codes change about this

The four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025, and the one that touches this arithmetic is the Code on Wages. Its definition of wages limits how much of a pay packet can sit in excluded allowances, which in practice pushes basic pay towards half of total remuneration.

Where an employer has been running a low basic and a large special allowance — which describes a great many Indian salary structures — lifting basic raises the provident fund and gratuity base. Contributions go up, retirement savings go up, and take-home goes down, with cost to company unchanged. Nobody is worse off in total; the monthly number just gets smaller.

How much smaller depends on detail that is still settling. Central and state rules under the codes have been coming through in stages, and employers have been restructuring at different speeds. Our piece on what the labour codes mean for payroll goes through the operational side, and the gratuity payout rules cover the qualifying-service question in more detail.

If you are the one writing the offer

Run the same three calculators in the same order, then do one more thing: put the take-home figure in the offer conversation yourself. The candidate is going to find it in week five regardless, and hearing it from you in week zero costs nothing and buys a great deal.

For the business side, what matters is that cost to company is a cash commitment with a shape. The provident fund goes out monthly. The gratuity provision does not leave the account until someone qualifies, which means it is a liability accumulating quietly unless you actually set the money aside. Tracking payroll outflow month by month in the Expense Tracker keeps the difference between what you have provided for and what you have funded visible.

If payroll has grown past the point where a spreadsheet and three calculators are enough — several states, a mix of structures, restructuring under the new codes — our payroll and compliance service runs it properly.
